Content:
Recall that a normally distributed random variable [MATH: X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)] has the probability density function

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \right)^2}.]

Content:
This probability density function can be written as

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = (2\pi)^{-{\color{red}1}/2 } ({\color{blue}\sigma^2})^{-1/2} \: \mathrm{exp}\left( -\frac{1}{2} (x-\mu) ({\color{blue}\sigma^2})^{-1} (x-\mu) \right).]

Content:
Let's compare this to the density function of a bivariate normal vector. First, we rewrite the joint density [MATH: f(x_1,x_2)] of the bivariate normal distribution as follows:

Content:
[MATH: f(x_{1}, x_{2})|= (1)/(2πsqrt(|Σ|))\exp(− (1)/(2)(X − μ)^{T}Σ^{− 1}(X − μ)); = (2π)^{− 1}|Σ|^{− 1/2}\exp(− (1)/(2)(X − μ)^{T}Σ^{− 1}(X − μ)); = (2π)^{− 2/2}|Σ|^{− 1/2}\exp(− (1)/(2)(X − μ)^{T}Σ^{− 1}(X − μ))]

Content:
By comparing the expressions for [MATH: f(x)] and [MATH: f(x_1,x_2),] we see that the bivariate normal distribution can be considered as a generalization of the normal distribution from the [MATH: {\color{red}1}]-dimensional case (when we have only one variable, [MATH: x]) to the [MATH: {\color{red}2}]-dimensional case (when we have two variables, [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2]).

Content:
This analogy will be particularly helpful when extending the bivariate normal distribution to more than two random variables.

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that if [MATH: \mathbf{X} = [X_1, X_2]^T] is a bivariate normal vector with mean vector [MATH: \boldsymbol{\mu}] and covariance matrix [MATH: \Sigma,] given by

[MATH: μ = (μ_{1}; μ_{2}), Σ = [σ_{1}^{2}|σ_{12}; σ_{21}|σ_{2}^{2}] = [σ_{1}^{2}|ρσ_{1}σ_{2}; ρσ_{1}σ_{2}|σ_{2}^{2}]]

where [MATH: \sigma^2_i = \textrm{Var}[X_i],] [MATH: \sigma_{12} = \textrm{Cov}[X_1,X_2],] and [MATH: \rho] is the correlation, then the joint probability density function of [MATH: \mathbf X] is [MATH: f(\mathbf x) = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{|\Sigma|}} \mathrm{exp}\left( -\dfrac 12(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol \mu)^T \,\Sigma^{-1} \,(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol \mu)\right)] and [MATH: |\Sigma|] denotes the determinant of [MATH: \Sigma.]

Using the given values of [MATH: \sigma^2_1, \sigma^2_2], and [MATH: \rho,] our covariance matrix is

[MATH: [9|(1)/(3) ⋅ sqrt(9) ⋅ sqrt(1); (1)/(3) ⋅ sqrt(9) ⋅ sqrt(1)|1]]

Therefore,

[MATH: |\Sigma| = 9\cdot 1 - 1\cdot 1 = 8.]

Substituting this value into our expression for the joint PDF, we obtain

[MATH: f(x)|= (1)/(2πsqrt(8))\exp(− (1)/(2)(x − μ)^{T}Σ^{− 1}(x − μ)); = (1)/(4 π 2)\exp(− (1)/(2)(x − μ)^{T}Σ^{− 1}(x − μ)).] Finally, [MATH: k=4\pi\sqrt 2.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let [MATH: \mathbf{X} = [X_1, X_2]^T] be two (dependent) random variables. We say that [MATH: \mathbf{X}] is a bivariate normal vector with mean vector [MATH: \boldsymbol{\mu}] and covariance matrix [MATH: \Sigma] if the joint probability density function of [MATH: \mathbf{X}] is given by

Content:
[MATH: f(x_1, x_2) = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{|\Sigma|}} \mathrm{exp}\left( -\dfrac 12(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)^T \,\Sigma^{-1} \,(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)\right)]

Content:
where

Content:
[MATH: μ = [μ_{1}; μ_{2}], Σ = [σ_{1}^{2}|σ_{12}; σ_{21}|σ_{2}^{2}] = [σ_{1}^{2}|ρσ_{1}σ_{2}; ρσ_{1}σ_{2}|σ_{2}^{2}],]

Content:
Here,

Content:
- [MATH: \sigma^2_1 = \textrm{Var}[X_1]] and [MATH: \sigma^2_2 = \textrm{Var}[X_2]] are the variances of [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2,]
- [MATH: \sigma_{12} = \sigma_{21} = \textrm{Cov}[X_1,X_2]] is the covariance of [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2],
- [MATH: \rho] is the linear correlation coefficient of [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2,] and
- [MATH: |\Sigma|] denotes the determinant of [MATH: \Sigma,] the covariance matrix.

Content:
A graph of a typical density function of a bivariate normal vector is depicted below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/becddc06fb28610a93d1f37c60dd4f1d]

Content:
This surface is often referred to as having a "bell shape."

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Normal Distribution vs. Bivariate Normal Distribution

Content:
Recall that a normally distributed random variable [MATH: X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)] has the probability density function

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \right)^2}.]

Content:
This probability density function can be written as

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = (2\pi)^{-{\color{red}1}/2 } ({\color{blue}\sigma^2})^{-1/2} \: \mathrm{exp}\left( -\frac{1}{2} (x-\mu) ({\color{blue}\sigma^2})^{-1} (x-\mu) \right).]

Content:
Let's compare this to the density function of a bivariate normal vector. First, we rewrite the joint density [MATH: f(x_1,x_2)] of the bivariate normal distribution as follows:

Content:
[MATH: f(x_{1}, x_{2})|= (1)/(2πsqrt(|Σ|))\exp(− (1)/(2)(X − μ)^{T}Σ^{− 1}(X − μ)); = (2π)^{− 1}|Σ|^{− 1/2}\exp(− (1)/(2)(X − μ)^{T}Σ^{− 1}(X − μ)); = (2π)^{− 2/2}|Σ|^{− 1/2}\exp(− (1)/(2)(X − μ)^{T}Σ^{− 1}(X − μ))]

Content:
By comparing the expressions for [MATH: f(x)] and [MATH: f(x_1,x_2),] we see that the bivariate normal distribution can be considered as a generalization of the normal distribution from the [MATH: {\color{red}1}]-dimensional case (when we have only one variable, [MATH: x]) to the [MATH: {\color{red}2}]-dimensional case (when we have two variables, [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2]).

Content:
This analogy will be particularly helpful when extending the bivariate normal distribution to more than two random variables.

---

Item 3 — Tutorial: Interpretation of Parameters in a Bivariate Normal Distribution

Content:
Let's consider a bivariate normal vector [MATH: \mathbf{X} = [X_1, X_2]^T] with the joint probability density function

Content:
[MATH: f(x_1, x_2) = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{|\Sigma|}} \mathrm{exp}\left( -\dfrac 12(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)^T \,\Sigma^{-1} \,(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)\right),]

Content:
where the mean vector [MATH: \boldsymbol{\mu}] and covariance matrix [MATH: \Sigma] are given by

Content:
[MATH: μ = [μ_{1}; μ_{2}], Σ = [σ_{1}^{2}|σ_{12}; σ_{21}|σ_{2}^{2}] = [σ_{1}^{2}|ρσ_{1}σ_{2}; ρσ_{1}σ_{2}|σ_{2}^{2}].]

Content:
Most of the parameters of the distribution can be interpreted geometrically on a corresponding graph of the probability density function:

Content:
- The mean vector [MATH: \boldsymbol{\mu}] gives the [MATH: xy]-coordinates of the peak.
- The correlation coefficient [MATH: \rho] defines how much the bell is squeezed towards the plane [MATH: y=x{:}]

- when [MATH: \rho \to 0,] the horizontal cross-sections are almost circular, while
- when [MATH: \rho \to 1,] the shape becomes more and more squeezed towards the plane [MATH: y=x.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/783789f61ba85060e43242de6ea0eeed]

Content:
- The variances [MATH: \sigma_1^2] and [MATH: \sigma_2^2] represent how much the curve is spread out along the principal axes [MATH: x_1=\mu_1] and [MATH: x_2=\mu_2{:}]

- when [MATH: \sigma_1^2] and [MATH: \sigma_2^2] are small, the bell shape is more "pointy," while
- for larger [MATH: \sigma_1^2] and [MATH: \sigma_2^2,] the bell shape is more "flat."

Content:
The level curves of the surface have equations of the form

Content:
[MATH: (\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)^T \,\Sigma^{-1} \,(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu) = \textrm{const},]

Content:
which represent ellipses centered at [MATH: (\mu_1,\mu_2).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/dcc9210c43f7ddc33f5e3e99a2d40a0a]

---

Item 4 — Example: The Joint PDF of a Bivariate Normal Random Variable

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: \mathbf{X} = [X_1, X_2]^T] be a bivariate normal random vector. The variances of [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] and their correlation coefficient are given by

[MATH: \sigma_1^2=9,\qquad \sigma_2^2 = 1, \qquad \rho = \dfrac1{3}.]

Given that the joint probability density function of [MATH: \mathbf X] is
[MATH: f(\mathbf x) = \dfrac1k\,\mathrm{exp}\left( -\dfrac 12(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol \mu)^T \,\Sigma^{-1} \,(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol \mu)\right),]

where [MATH: \boldsymbol{\mu}] is the mean vector and [MATH: \Sigma] is the corresponding covariance matrix, find the value of [MATH: k.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that if [MATH: \mathbf{X} = [X_1, X_2]^T] is a bivariate normal vector with mean vector [MATH: \boldsymbol{\mu}] and covariance matrix [MATH: \Sigma,] given by

[MATH: μ = (μ_{1}; μ_{2}), Σ = [σ_{1}^{2}|σ_{12}; σ_{21}|σ_{2}^{2}] = [σ_{1}^{2}|ρσ_{1}σ_{2}; ρσ_{1}σ_{2}|σ_{2}^{2}]]

where [MATH: \sigma^2_i = \textrm{Var}[X_i],] [MATH: \sigma_{12} = \textrm{Cov}[X_1,X_2],] and [MATH: \rho] is the correlation, then the joint probability density function of [MATH: \mathbf X] is
[MATH: f(\mathbf x) = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{|\Sigma|}} \mathrm{exp}\left( -\dfrac 12(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol \mu)^T \,\Sigma^{-1} \,(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol \mu)\right)]
and [MATH: |\Sigma|] denotes the determinant of [MATH: \Sigma.]

Using the given values of [MATH: \sigma^2_1, \sigma^2_2], and [MATH: \rho,] our covariance matrix is

[MATH: [9|(1)/(3) ⋅ sqrt(9) ⋅ sqrt(1); (1)/(3) ⋅ sqrt(9) ⋅ sqrt(1)|1]]

Therefore,

[MATH: |\Sigma| = 9\cdot 1 - 1\cdot 1 = 8.]

Substituting this value into our expression for the joint PDF, we obtain

[MATH: f(x)|= (1)/(2πsqrt(8))\exp(− (1)/(2)(x − μ)^{T}Σ^{− 1}(x − μ)); = (1)/(4 π 2)\exp(− (1)/(2)(x − μ)^{T}Σ^{− 1}(x − μ)).]
Finally, [MATH: k=4\pi\sqrt 2.]

Item 7 — Tutorial: Linear Combinations of Normal Random Variables From Bivariate Distributions

Content:
A linear combination of coordinates of a bivariate normal random vector generates a (one-dimensional) normal distribution:

Content:
> If [MATH: \mathbf{X} = [X_1, X_2]^T] is a bivariate normal random vector with mean vector [MATH: \boldsymbol{\mu}] and covariance matrix [MATH: \Sigma,] given by
> [MATH: μ = [μ_{1}; μ_{2}], Σ = [σ_{1}^{2}|σ_{12}; σ_{21}|σ_{2}^{2}],]
> then the random variable [MATH: Y,] defined as
> [MATH: Y= aX_1 + bX_2]
> is a normally distributed random variable for all values of [MATH: a] and [MATH: b.] Furthermore, we have that
> [MATH: E[Y]|= aμ_{1} + bμ_{2},; Var[Y]|= a^{2}σ_{1}^{2} + b^{2}σ_{2}^{2} + 2abσ_{12}.]

Item 8 — Example: Linear Combinations of Elements From a Bivariate Normal Random Variable

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that if [MATH: \mathbf{X} = [X_1, X_2]^T] is a bivariate normal random vector with mean vector [MATH: \boldsymbol{\mu}] and covariance matrix [MATH: \Sigma,] given by
[MATH: μ = [μ_{1}; μ_{2}], Σ = [σ_{1}^{2}|σ_{12}; σ_{21}|σ_{2}^{2}],]
then the random variable [MATH: Y,] defined as

[MATH: Y= aX_1 + bX_2]

is a normally distributed random variable for all values of [MATH: a] and [MATH: b,] where

[MATH: E[Y]|= aμ_{1} + bμ_{2},; Var[Y]|= a^{2}σ_{1}^{2} + b^{2}σ_{2}^{2} + 2abσ_{12}.]

In our case, we have [MATH: \mu_1 = 2] and [MATH: \mu_2 = -1.] Therefore,
[MATH: E[Y]|= E[3X_{1} + X_{2}]; = 3E[X_{1}] + E[X_{2}]; = 3 ⋅ μ_{1} + μ_{2}; = 3 ⋅ 2 + (− 1); = 5.]

Also, we have [MATH: \sigma_1^2 = 4, \sigma_2^2 = 7,] and [MATH: \sigma_{12} = \sigma_{21} = -3.] Therefore,
[MATH: Var[Y]|= Var[3X_{1} + X_{2}]; = 3^{2} ⋅ 4 + 1^{2} ⋅ 7 + 2 ⋅ 3 ⋅ 1 ⋅ (− 3); = 36 + 7 − 18; = 25.]

Item 11 — Tutorial: The Multivariate Normal Distribution

Content:
Earlier, we compared the PDF of [MATH: X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2),] given by

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = (2\pi)^{-{\color{red}1}/2 } ({\color{blue}\sigma^2})^{-1/2} \: \mathrm{exp}\left( -\frac{1}{2} (x-\mu) ({\color{blue}\sigma^2})^{-1} (x-\mu) \right).]

Content:
and the joint PDF of a bivariate normal distribution [MATH: \mathbf X = [X_1,X_2]^T] with mean vector [MATH: \boldsymbol\mu] and covariance matrix [MATH: \Sigma,] given by

Content:
[MATH: f(x_1, x_2) = (2\pi)^{-{\color{red}2}/2} {\color{blue}|\Sigma|}^{-1/2} \: \mathrm{exp}\left( -\dfrac 12(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)^T \,{\color{blue}\Sigma}^{-1} \,(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)\right).]

Content:
We can generalize this for an arbitrary number of variables [MATH: {\color{red}p},] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_p) = (2\pi)^{-{\color{red}p}/2} {\color{blue}|\Sigma|}^{-1/2} \: \mathrm{exp}\left( -\dfrac 12(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)^T \,{\color{blue}\Sigma}^{-1} \,(\mathbf X - \boldsymbol \mu)\right)]

Content:
The function [MATH: f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_p)] is called the multivariate normal density function. A random vector [MATH: \mathbf X = [X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_p]^T] with this joint density function is said to follow a multivariate normal distribution.

Content:
Similar to the bivariate case, we can consider linear combinations of coordinates of multivariate normal random vectors:

Content:
> If [MATH: \mathbf{X} = [X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_k]^T] is a multivariate normal random vector with mean vector [MATH: \boldsymbol{\mu}] and covariance matrix [MATH: \Sigma,] then the random variable [MATH: Y,] defined as [MATH: Y= \mathbf c^T \mathbf X = \sum_{i=1}^k c_i X_i] is a normally distributed random variable, where [MATH: \mathbf c] is any [MATH: k\times 1] column vector, and

Content:
[MATH: E[Y]|= c^{T}μ,; Var[Y]|= c^{T}Σc.]

Content:
Notice that the expression for the variance is a quadratic form.
